contentHtml:
CNCF projects highlighted in this post

An open source adventure featuring Kubernetes, agent-substrate, kagent, AI agents, drones, and more!

Just 30 seconds before going live for the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 closing keynote, “Cloud Native Without Limits: What Can AI Agents Do for Us?”, while Abdel Sghiouar was introducing me, Cory Jett leaned over and whispered: “The drone isn’t connecting to the controller!” 😱

A heart-stopping moment!

Thankfully, a quick reboot saved the day. And then came the moment I’ll never forget: walking onto the stage with a live drone following right behind me! 🚁✨

And when I finally walked off stage, all the nervousness and anxiety were gone. I was just SO happy! What a feeling! ❤️

On-stage live demo with the drone and big screens

🥋 From Amsterdam to Salt Lake City: Never give up!

After my Amsterdam keynote, where the drone camera failed, Christian Dussol taught me the martial arts lesson of “Osu” (never give up! 🥋💪). That lesson stuck with me, and I wanted to push the boundaries even further in Salt Lake City.

Striking the “Osu” posture after the Amsterdam keynote

While brainstorming with Allison Price around our theme, “Cloud Native Without Limits,” we asked ourselves: What if we could let the audience experience what it’s like to fly and build something live on stage, powered by AI agents?

Of course, bringing a live drone indoors isn’t exactly plug-and-play. There was quite a bit of work behind the scenes!

🛠️ Behind the scenes: Making the impossible possible

A few challenges we had to tackle:

🛩️ Regulatory compliance: Back in August, we learned that an FAA Part 107-certified remote pilot was required for our indoor drone operation. Cory stepped up, completed the necessary training in just one week, and saved the demo! 🙌

Teaser at the venue 😅

🏠 Home testing: I got propeller guards so I could safely experiment with code, test flight paths, and practice flying indoors at home. Let’s just say my house became a mini drone testing lab!

Flight testing at home with propeller guards

But this demo was about much more than flying a drone. We wanted to show what real-time agentic execution looks like, with the right guardrails, sandboxing, and observability in place.

🤖 Under the hood: The Cloud Native technologies behind the drone

Here’s what powered the experience:

🤖 Agents: Running on CNCF Sanbox projects agent-substrate, and kagent providing an opinionated layer for building and running agents.

🔐Then AAIF Growth project agentgateway: Playing multiple roles:

  • LLM gateway: Rate limiting and controlling access to models.
  • Egress gateway (as part of agent-substrate): Enforcing sandbox and network access policies.
  • MCP gateway: Handling authentication and authorization for Model Context Protocol tool calls with an Identity Provider, for example, Keycloak.

📊 OpenTelemetry and Jaeger: Providing end-to-end observability across agent execution through agentgateway and agent-substrate, including rate-limiting errors, the duration of each tool call, and where agents spend most of their time.

All coming together to make an AI-powered physical experience happen, live on stage!

The moment when it all comes together live on stage

💜 A big Thank You & what’s next? 🇪🇸

The community’s response was incredible! It’s exciting to see how far we’ve come as an industry, bringing AI models, agentic AI, and cloud native technologies together to make things possible that would have seemed like science fiction just a few years ago.

A massive THANK YOU to my manager, Idit Levine, for her unwavering support; Cory Jett, for making the drone flight possible; Allison Price, for brainstorming this adventure with me; Jonathan Bryce, for loving the drone idea when I casually brought it up during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2025; Elna Vogel, for making sure we had the required insurance.

And of course, a huge shout-out to the entire event and technical teams who helped bring this adventure to life! ❤️

Last but definitely not least, THANK YOU to the agent-substrate, kagent, and agentgateway communities! They answered every question I threw at them, responded incredibly quickly, and were always ready to jump in and debug live if needed. I couldn’t have pulled this off without you! 💜

My #substrate-dev team CNCF slack

📺 Missed the keynote? Catch the full recording!

Now, I’m officially wrapping up the Drone 2 chapter and already looking forward to building something fresh for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon 2027 in Barcelona! 🇪🇸

So, what physical objects or hardware should we hack on next? Drones have had their moment. What’s next? What could we build that I haven’t even imagined yet? 🙂

summary: IBM Research 在 Hugging Face 官方博客介绍如何用其开源智能体框架 CUGA 构建面向印度语系（Indic）语言的语音智能体。文章属于官方工程实践分享，聚焦 CUGA 框架在语音智能体场景中的搭建方法。

contentHtml:
Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

The use case: a Farm Assistant

A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:

  1. Listens and turns the speech into text.
  2. Searches a 154-page agricultural handbook, which is written in English.
  3. Answers in two to four spoken sentences, in the language the question was asked in, using only what the handbook says.
  4. Speaks the answer back and shows the source pages, so the answer can be checked.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

Where CUGA fits

CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:

  • One agent, any model. Switch between watsonx and OpenAI with one setting.
  • The knowledge engine. Parse a PDF, chunk it, embed it, and search it locally with agent.knowledge.search().
  • Conversation threads. Each question gets a fresh thread, so one person's language or context never leaks into another's.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

audio ──▶ speech-to-text ──▶ knowledge.search ──▶ CUGA (grounded answer) ──▶ text-to-speech ──▶ audio

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

The hard part is not the voice

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

Making it sound right and keeping it safe

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:

  • Write for the ear. Markdown, bullet points, citation tags and bracketed translations such as "millet (बाजरा)" all sound wrong when read aloud. The prompt asks the model not to produce them, and a light formatter strips any that slip through before speech.
  • Keep guardrails cheap. Simple input checks catch obvious off-topic questions. If one gets through, the model starts its reply with OFF_TOPIC, and the app swaps in a polite redirect. No second LLM call, so the voice path stays fast.
  • Ground every answer. The model sees only the retrieved passages, is told not to use outside knowledge, and the page sources are shown to the user.
  • Keep keys out of the server. With the Sarvam option, the browser talks to Sarvam directly. The server receives only text and never sees the user's key.

Try it

You do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:

CUGA Apps on Hugging Face →

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

Beyond farming: Scaling for Bharat

Nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

This approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

title: 你的 OpenTelemetry 管道正在成为性能瓶颈吗？
originalTitle: Is your OpenTelemetry pipeline becoming a performance bottleneck?
summary: CNCF 博客发布 Cloud Native Days Austria 2026 演讲回顾《How to Defeat OTel's Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead》，聚焦可观测性管道中容易被忽视的采集性能开销问题。演讲探讨 OpenTelemetry 管道何时会成为性能瓶颈及其应对方法。
context: 采集开销是可观测性落地的隐性成本，对大规模使用 OpenTelemetry 的团队有直接参考价值。
contentHtml:
Posted on November 17, 2026 by Diana Todea (CNCF Ambassador, OpenTelemetry Documentation approver, Romanian Localization maintainer)

At Cloud Native Days Austria 2026, I presented a talk called How to Defeat OTel’s Silent Killer: The Performance Overhead, exploring a problem that is easy to overlook when building observability pipelines: the cost of collecting telemetry itself.

OpenTelemetry has become a cornerstone of cloud-native observability, providing standardized APIs, SDKs, and tooling for generating, collecting, processing, and exporting metrics, logs, and traces. However, instrumentation and telemetry processing are not free. Every span created, attribute attached, and batch exported consumes resources.

As applications scale, poorly configured telemetry pipelines can introduce significant CPU usage, memory pressure, network traffic, and storage costs. In some cases, the infrastructure responsible for observing a system can become a performance problem of its own.

The good news is that much of this overhead can be understood, measured, and reduced without sacrificing the visibility engineers depend on.

Where does OpenTelemetry overhead come from?

When discussing OpenTelemetry performance, we often focus on the application SDK. However, the cost extends beyond instrumentation.

The entire telemetry pipeline contributes to resource consumption, from generating spans and collecting metrics to processing, exporting, and storing data.

Instrumentation overhead is also workload-dependent. Two applications using the same instrumentation libraries can experience very different results depending on request throughput, attribute volume, runtime behavior, and the number of spans generated per request.

This is why relying on a single overhead percentage can be misleading. Instead, we should examine CPU consumption, memory usage, application latency, telemetry volume, and the behavior of the Collector under load.

There is also an important trade-off between application safety and telemetry completeness. When a pipeline becomes overloaded, backpressure and memory safeguards can protect the application and OpenTelemetry Collector, but they may also lead to rejected or dropped telemetry.

The objective is not simply to minimize resource consumption. It is to maintain useful observability while keeping its operational cost predictable.

Investigating the Collector: five common configuration problems

For my demonstration, I used Telemetrygen, an OpenTelemetry utility that generates synthetic telemetry, to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption.

The investigation focused on five common sources of unnecessary overhead.

1. Inefficient batching

Exporting small amounts of telemetry frequently can increase serialization work, export requests, and network overhead.

The OpenTelemetry Collector groups telemetry inside the exporter’s sending queue before transmitting it downstream, helping amortize this work across larger payloads. (Note: Historically, this was handled by a standalone batch processor, which is now deprecated in favor of built-in exporter batching).

However, batching parameters should reflect the actual workload. Larger batches are not automatically better: they can increase buffering requirements and affect export latency.

exporters:
  otlp_grpc:
    endpoint: "otel-backend:4317"
    sending_queue:
      enabled: true
      sizer: items       
      queue_size: 100000 
      batch:
        enabled: true
        min_size: 8192
        flush_timeout: 200ms

Configuring batch inside an exporter’s sending_queue groups spans, metrics, or logs before forwarding them downstream, improving compression efficiency and durability while reducing export overhead. Batches are sent when a configured size threshold is reached or a timeout expires.

In this example, min_size: 8192 triggers an export when the batch reaches 8,192 items, while flush_timeout: 200ms triggers an export regardless of batch size. Once batching is enabled, these values are the Collector’s documented defaults, not universal performance recommendations. (Note: Because unbatched requests enter the queue first in this architecture, this example switches sizer from the default requests to items with a queue_size of 100000 to prevent smaller, unbatched bursts from overflowing the queue).

The important point is to measure how batching affects resource consumption and throughput rather than relying on example configurations.

2. Unnecessary resource attributes

Resource attributes provide valuable context about the systems producing telemetry. But collecting and forwarding attributes that nobody uses can increase payload sizes and downstream processing costs.

For example, an application might need host.name, host.arch, and os.type for troubleshooting, but not detailed hardware information such as host.cpu.model.name or host.cpu.cache.l2.size.

The OpenTelemetry Collector’s resource detection processor allows engineers to configure which system attributes are collected. Disabling unnecessary attributes can reduce telemetry volume and processing overhead, although the impact on storage and cardinality depends on the backend.

A practical example: Keep the hostname and operating system type, but disable CPU model and cache metadata when those details are not needed for troubleshooting.

3. Aggressive receiver polling

Infrastructure receivers collect metrics at configured intervals, often independently of application traffic.

Polling host metrics, container statistics, databases, and network services every few seconds creates continuous work even when applications are relatively idle.

Increasing collection intervals from 10 to 30 seconds, where operational requirements permit, can reduce collection frequency and associated overhead.

This introduces a trade-off: lower polling frequency means less temporal resolution. The appropriate interval depends on how quickly a metric changes and how it is used for troubleshooting or alerting.

4. Exporting every trace

Not every successful request needs to produce a trace that is retained.

Exporting all traces can consume significant bandwidth, Collector resources, and backend capacity, particularly in high-throughput applications.

Sampling provides a way to control this volume.

Head-based sampling makes decisions early, reducing downstream work. Tail-based sampling makes decisions after observing more of a trace, enabling policies that retain errors or other diagnostically interesting requests.

These policies retain traces with an error status and probabilistically sample 5% of traces, including potentially some additional error traces. However, tail sampling is not free. It requires buffering trace data until a decision can be made, introducing additional memory and processing overhead. 

Choosing a sampling strategy means balancing cost, diagnostic value, and the resources needed to make sampling decisions.

5. Memory safeguards applied too late

The OpenTelemetry Collector includes a memory_limiter processor to help manage memory pressure.

Processor ordering matters. When enrichment and transformation processors run before memory limiting, the Collector may perform additional work on telemetry that is subsequently refused under memory pressure.

Memory limiting is a protective mechanism rather than a performance optimization in itself. Its purpose is to improve stability under pressure, not necessarily to reduce CPU consumption during normal operation. Placing the memory limiter early in the pipeline helps apply safeguards before more expensive processing. 

It is important to understand that the memory limiter is not a substitute for appropriate resource limits or capacity planning. It can refuse incoming data when memory pressure becomes excessive, and receivers must handle this behavior correctly to avoid unnecessary telemetry loss.

From local experiments to production architecture

Optimizing a single Collector is only part of the solution.

In Kubernetes, telemetry workloads can fluctuate significantly as applications scale, deployments change, and traffic increases. A Collector configuration that performs well under synthetic load may behave differently in production.

Here are some architectural practices that can help address these challenges.

  1. Separate collection from centralized processing. A two-tier architecture can use lightweight edge Collectors for local collection and gateway Collectors for more expensive processing. This allows different parts of the pipeline to scale according to their workloads.
  2. Control telemetry volume early. Filtering unnecessary attributes, removing unneeded data, and avoiding excessive cardinality can reduce the amount of information processed and transferred downstream. These decisions should preserve the context required for debugging and correlation.
  3. Plan for memory pressure and backend outages. Kubernetes memory limits, Collector memory safeguards, bounded queues, and retry mechanisms serve different purposes. Persistent queues can improve resilience during temporary backend failures, but they still require capacity planning and cannot guarantee delivery under every failure scenario.
  4. Scale with signal-specific requirements in mind. Horizontal scaling can increase throughput, but stateful processing requires additional consideration. Tail sampling, for example, generally requires spans belonging to the same trace to reach the same processing instance.

These architectural decisions are just as important as tuning individual processors.

Don’t forget the instrumentation

One of the most effective optimizations happens before telemetry reaches the Collector.

Instrumentation should answer meaningful operational questions rather than collect everything simply because it is possible. Excessive spans, high-cardinality attributes, and unnecessary instrumentation can increase resource consumption throughout the entire pipeline.

For metrics, attributes containing unbounded values such as unique request IDs can create large numbers of distinct time series. For traces and logs, excessive attributes and events increase payload sizes and may affect backend processing or indexing costs.

Why I chose Telemetrygen for my demo

When preparing my performance investigation, I initially considered using the official OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop. While it is an excellent environment for exploring instrumentation across microservices, its multiple applications, databases, and supporting services introduce additional CPU and memory consumption.

For this experiment, I wanted to isolate the Collector’s performance overhead without the background noise of a complete application environment.

Instead, I chose Telemetrygen, a lightweight utility for generating synthetic traces, metrics, and logs at controlled rates.

In my OpenTelemetry performance overhead demo, I used synthetic telemetry to investigate how Collector configuration affects resource consumption. The demonstration walks through common inefficiencies, including missing batching, unnecessary resource attributes, aggressive receiver polling, excessive trace export, and memory limiter placement, showing how targeted configuration changes can improve pipeline efficiency.

This approach helped isolate Collector behavior, but it is only one part of the performance picture. For understanding instrumentation overhead inside real applications, a complete environment such as Astronomy Shop remains valuable.

Exploring instrumentation further

Reducing overhead starts with understanding what telemetry an application generates and why. The official OpenTelemetry instrumentation documentation introduces automatic and manual instrumentation, while the sampling documentation explains how to control trace volume. These are useful starting points for reviewing instrumentation decisions before optimizing the Collector itself.

For engineers interested in investigating performance further, the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation covers pipeline configuration and processing. The OpenTelemetry community is also a good place to discuss performance challenges. The Collector SIG focuses on Collector architecture, performance, and configuration, with discussions taking place in the #otel-collector channel on CNCF Slack.

For questions about instrumentation overhead in a specific programming language, the corresponding language SIG is a better starting point. The OpenTelemetry community page provides information about SIGs, public meetings, and how to get involved.

Making performance part of observability design

OpenTelemetry overhead is not a single problem with a single configuration fix.

It is the combined effect of instrumentation decisions, data volume, processor configuration, export behavior, and infrastructure architecture.

The most useful lesson from this investigation is that observability pipelines should be measured and optimized like any other production system.

Start with controlled benchmarks. Understand where resources are consumed. Introduce configuration changes individually, and evaluate their impact on CPU, memory, latency, throughput, and telemetry loss.

Most importantly, treat example configurations as starting points rather than production-ready defaults.

OpenTelemetry gives us the tools to understand complex distributed systems. With thoughtful instrumentation, careful pipeline configuration, and appropriate scaling strategies, we can ensure that collecting this information does not become an unnecessary burden on the systems we are trying to observe.

title: Anthropic 将 Messages API 从 Python 迁移到 Rust
originalTitle: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
summary: Anthropic 工程团队将其 Messages API 从 Python 迁移到 Rust，并公开了这次核心 API 重写的迁移过程。文章记录了从语言选型到落地迁移的具体做法与工程经验。
context: Anthropic 官方工程实践，展示头部 AI 公司如何为其核心 API 接口做语言级重写。
contentHtml:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.

But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything. Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it.

We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged.

In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development.

Why migrate?

We built the Messages API in 2023 and wrote it in Python, which was widely used internally for much of our research code. At first, it was simple. The Messages API passed requests to the model and sent back what the model wrote. (One engineer at the time called it “basically a request forwarder.”) But as the Messages API became more capable and deeply integrated with our codebases, it also developed shared dependencies with Python libraries that were owned by our research and inference teams, which made it hard to move. If we ever wanted to move to another language, it would mean building logging, metrics, and tools all over again.

This calculus gradually began to change. By late 2025, every Messages API request had to be validated, converted into the prompt, tokenized, and screened by our safety classifiers. As each reply arrived, the stream of tokens had to be sorted into text, thinking, and tool calls, and Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task. Traffic eventually grew far beyond what the initial Python service was built for (Figure 1), and we quickly needed to find a way to make the service much more efficient.

Incremental or all at once?

Full rewrites of large production systems are often approached cautiously, for at least two reasons. First, there is no guarantee that test suites cover 100% of production code behavior, and rewriting it is risky. Second, the sheer effort required often makes such work intractable. (In 2024, after one of our engineers suggested migrating to Go or Rust, another temporarily settled the question: “We are not rewriting the API in go or rust!”)

The standard advice if you’re looking for performance gains is thus to rewrite only the parts that are slowing the system down, so that’s where we started. In Rust, we rewrote the code that parses a model’s output and called it from Python. This reduced the API’s CPU usage by about 8% to 10%. However, incremental solutions often incur added complexity, and it’s important to make sure that incremental improvements justify those costs. In our case, the gains didn’t justify the added complexity. Each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times (Figure 2), creating new sources of overhead.

As Claude became increasingly capable, we began to question whether the usual reasons to avoid a full migration still held. The effort required to undertake the project was dropping fast: by May 2026, Claude was writing more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged. We wondered if Claude could now help us write code that would empirically capture every behavior and fix in the production system. But the question became: how could we verify that the behavior of our migration was correct? Verification, not generation, had become the bottleneck.

How we verified the migration

General approaches

To verify the migration, we first needed to define what “correct” meant. You can do this in a few ways (Figure 3). If you’re lucky, you can simply write a rule. A theorem in mathematics is a precise statement, and a proof assistant (like Lean) can check each step of a proof against a fixed set of rules. Other times—and more frequently in software engineering—you define “correct” with a set of examples, like tests. For instance, when Bun moved from Zig to Rust, its test suite was written in TypeScript, so the same tests could judge both versions. In our case, neither approach was sufficient, so we used the existing system as an oracle to test parity during the migration. In this case, our existing system (the Messages API) kept changing. We were releasing new models and shipping new features regularly, which made the definition of “correct” a moving target.

Tests

Tests were the easiest place for us to start, since we already had an existing set of about 700 integration tests. However, two problems limited our ability to trust them to verify the correctness of a migration as high stakes as this (Figure 4).

The tests were coupled to the Python implementation. An integration test sends a request, then checks the reply and what was sent to other services. Our tests ran the Python API inside the test’s process and mocked services, like billing and rate limiting, in Python’s memory. The tests had to change along with the code, and Claude helped with both. Now, a “pass” could mean that the code was right, or that the test had been changed in a way that let wrong code through. We saw this happen: when we audited the ported tests, we found more than 100 weakened assertions.

The tests were incomplete. The Messages API has dozens of features, and there are far too many configurations to test them exhaustively. Just 20 binary options make over a million combinations—that translates to 12 days of tests at a second each, for one model, before we even vary the prompts inside them. In practice, engineers test a subset that tries to approximate production, but that process inevitably misses cases. Some projects, like Bun, have an independent suite that’s extensive enough to judge a rewrite. Many production services don’t; what counts as correct depends as much on how they behave as on what’s in their tests or documentation.

Detecting parity with production

Production data is sometimes “the only true test” that new code behaves like the old code. Running requests through old and new code and comparing the results is often called shadowing. To understand what we needed to compare, it helps to walk through what happens to a single request on the Messages API (Figure 5). The API validates each request, converts it into a prompt a model can read (the prompt for inference), tokenizes it, and runs it through safety classifiers. A model then writes a reply, one token at a time. On the output side, the API sorts those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, streams them to the customer, and counts usage for limits and billing.

The migration covered both the input and output paths. Some differences were obvious, such as when the Rust API rejected a request that Python had accepted. But many were subtle. For instance, if the Rust API left out part of a prompt, the request would still succeed and the model would still answer, though sometimes with minor differences.

Our Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April, yet only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (Figure 6). The gap came partly from cases in production traffic that our tests didn’t cover. For example, when Python writes JSON tool calls, it escapes certain characters (e.g., an emoji) by replacing them with text codes. Rust wrote those characters as is, so the two prompts differed by a few bytes. Production also weighted bugs differently. In a test suite, each case counts once, but in live traffic, a bug will show up in each request where it’s triggered, which means a single common bug can cause many mismatches.

Common tools for shadowing often assume that a request can safely run twice, or that a service is deterministic. These assumptions didn’t apply in our case. We had to ensure that a request only counted once toward a customer’s limits and bill. In addition, Claude is nondeterministic, meaning that replies can differ for the same input (Figure 7). To address this, we ran the model once and replayed the model output to Rust.

With both versions working from the same model output, we still had to compare every stage before and after the model call, and the results had to match exactly. In many systems, bad input causes an error somewhere down the stack. But since Claude accepts almost any prompt, even a small deviation can change its reply without triggering an error. We compared each step before and after the model call, so that we could pin down any deviation that might change what a customer received.

It was important to us to do this in a way that protected user privacy. To do that we had to work without reading user requests or Claude’s replies to them, which means we couldn’t easily see where the Rust and Python versions of the API differed. So instead of looking at text, we recorded the shape of each difference, such as where it happened in the service and how big it was. We did this using a few different approaches:

  • Checkpointing. Both API versions handle a request using the same steps: accept or reject it, resolve its settings, build the prompt. Every step produces some result, such as an error or the pieces of the prompt, that we could compare step by step, and within the prompt, piece by piece. The first place they differed indicated roughly where the migration code differed from production code (Figure 8).
  • Fingerprint. Once we knew roughly where each diff resided, we still needed a way to distinguish one bug from another. We recorded where each difference began in the prompt, as well as the length difference between the two versions. Combined with the step and piece of the prompt isolated in checkpointing, we found that bugs presented with a specific fingerprint. That is, one bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects (Figure 9). We could then group errors by fingerprint, which helped us triage the fixes.

The result was a shadowing system that produced a small record of each difference between our Rust and Python APIs. Here is an example, with made-up values:

We could then pass this record to an agent to fix it.

Verification loops

Each request that differed left a record in our logs. A single bug could produce hundreds of thousands of nearly identical diff records. Rather than send each to an agent, we ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by which fields differed, then alerted a coordinating Claude agent only when it saw a new kind of record. This coordinator assigned a worker agent to own each new kind of record. It also created a new thread in a shared Slack channel where human engineers could follow along and steer it when necessary.

To tackle the many bugs, we set up a series of verification loops. A fast inner loop gave agents a sandbox in which they could test ideas and propose fixes. A slower outer loop then validated fixes in production. In addition, a memory loop recorded any mistakes along the way, saving them so that agents could learn over time (Figure 10).

Inner loop

When we first started testing this in April, we gave each agent a record that showed where the Rust and Python versions differed. Agents would guess the root cause from the code and open a pull request. Once the fix was reviewed and merged, they deployed it to staging, a preproduction copy of the Rust API where we ran the same shadow comparison on test traffic. The agents checked whether the difference was eliminated. Since every hypothesis needed a review and a deployment, feedback was taking hours or days.

We needed agents to get a signal from verification much sooner, so we moved them into their own workspace. We redesigned the inner loop so that agents could have a place to test ideas quickly and fail safely. Each agent ran in a cloud sandbox with both codebases and fast, local checks for what happens before and after the model call. The input check took a request, built the prompt that each version would send to the model, and showed what differed. Because this check never actually called the model, comparing the versions took under a second. We later added an output check, which ran both versions against a fake model. The output check passed a scripted reply, such as a tool call, through each version and compared the results.

The main limitation was that agents could only see the fingerprint, not the request behind each record. So an agent would hypothesize what had caused the difference, then write its own request or model reply to try to reproduce the difference. Since each agent was writing these itself, it could read both results in full. If the results matched, its guess was wrong and the agent tried again. If they differed the same way the record described, the agent edited the Rust until the two versions matched, then added a test that failed on the old code and passed on the new (Figure 11).

The seam between the inner and outer loops was a good checkpoint for human review. Inside the sandbox, a wrong guess cost an agent only a few seconds and had no impact on users. Agents could iterate on their own. We allowed a fix to cross into the outer loop only after it had undergone PR review; this allowed engineers to focus their attention on proposed fixes (rather than on guesses) and on the questions the verifiers couldn’t answer, such as whether a difference between the Rust and Python APIs was the result of a bug or a deliberate change.

Agents posted their fixes and evidence to their Slack threads for engineers to review. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences between the Rust and Python APIs came from web search. The production API retrieved the web search tool’s description from an internal service. The Rust API didn’t call this service yet, so the tool description was missing from the prompts. An agent proposed a shortcut to copy the text into files that would be readable by Rust. The prompts then matched, and the fix passed the local verifier. But an engineer turned it down because it didn’t solve the problem: Rust would still need to call the service before launch, at which point the workaround would be thrown out (Figure 12).

But the verifier rewarded matching outputs, and the agent found the cheapest way to produce them. A verifier can tell an agent whether the outputs matched, but not whether the fix is good enough to ship. That’s why human review was an important gate.

Outer loop

In the inner loop, agents debugged differences and proposed fixes. At the seam between the inner loop and the outer loop, engineers reviewed the proposed fixes, gave feedback, and approved them to deploy. The outer loop then compared Rust API deployments with and without each fix.

To make that comparison fair, we logged facts about each request we compared, but not its text, including which model and API features it used—for example, prompt caching, tools, or extended thinking. These details let agents compare requests of the same kind (Figure 13) and ask how often the bug’s fingerprint appeared on builds with and without the fix. This way, agents could monitor the new builds for the bug.

We designed the outer loop to catch problems that the inner loop missed. The inner loop simulated production quickly but imperfectly: agents could test a hypothesis in seconds, but only on requests they had written, and with a local verifier that wasn’t always configured exactly like production.

This means that sometimes a fix passed in the sandbox and production still showed the difference. The agent assigned to the bug would either see the difference in the new build’s records, or be alerted by the coordinating agent. It then went back to the inner loop and used that evidence to form a new hypothesis.

Memory loop

The inner and outer loops fixed one difference at a time. The memory loop improved how agents made those fixes. We didn’t want engineers to have to make the same correction twice, so we recorded what came out of reviews and agents’ own work and applied it to every agent that followed.

For example, when an engineer turned down the web search shortcut (Figure 12), the agent saved a note to memory explaining the decision, the reason for it, and the correct fix, which was to have Rust call the service that supplies tool descriptions.

Building that call took our team weeks, and in the meantime the bug kept producing records. Some had new fingerprints, because the missing text fell at other positions in the prompt or belonged to another tool that used the same service. Agents checked the memory note, recognized the known bug, and linked those records to it, instead of writing another workaround (Figure 14).

Other lessons became general rules for porting and writing Rust. After one agent guessed at Python’s behavior, an engineer made it a rule to port exactly what Python did. An agent then compared the existing code with that rule and found seven more places where the port had relied on a guess.

In June, an agent also went through about 60 of the team’s review comments, grouped the recurring problems and proposed rules, which an engineer edited and approved for CLAUDE.md (Figure 14).

The memory loop also encoded some lessons in permanent checks. This included new tests that failed when Rust drifted from Python, lints that banned patterns reviewers kept flagging, and later a merge check that required anyone changing the Python code to make a matching change in Rust or request an exemption.

Looking ahead

It’s increasingly feasible to migrate production systems with Claude, either for better performance or security, without taking an API offline or slowing feature development. Now that the hard part is no longer writing new code, we need to build sufficient confidence that the new system behaves like the old one.

The usual approach to migration is a bit like rebuilding the Ship of Theseus, in which the old ship was replaced plank by plank. Generally it’s been possible to replace planks while the ship still sails, but changing too many planks at once requires coming into dock. To fully stretch the metaphor, Claude now makes it possible to build an identically functioning ship alongside the first—even as the first keeps sailing and having its planks replaced. Agents kept the new ship in step as the old one changed, and we kept checking that the two behaved the same. Once we trusted that they did, we moved the passengers over a few at a time. The new ship sails faster and more efficiently than the old one.

Lessons learned

Verification is the new bottleneck. Previously, large software projects like migrations were hard to justify because they took too much effort and carried too much risk. But if writing code is no longer the bottleneck, the main constraint becomes how quickly you can verify results. In general, ambition can be increased as long as there’s a way for Claude to verify correctness.

Verification is how you earn confidence. In math, we use a proof assistant to verify that each step of a proof Claude wrote is valid. For software, tests or formal verification can help us gain similar confidence. But when these checks aren’t enough, a production system itself can also be a verifier.

Carefully design the verification signal. A verifier provides a signal that Claude can act on. We can calibrate this signal to show Claude where things went wrong. Where a proof assistant points to the failing step or a test names the failing case, a production system often offers no such signal by default. Much of our effort for this project went to building such a signal. In this case, checkpoints located each difference in the code and fingerprints helped tell one bug from another.

Build loops that let Claude autonomously act on the signal. Our inner loop was fast and ran locally in a sandbox. Agents tested hypotheses in seconds using requests they wrote themselves. The outer loop was slower and checked fixes on shadowed production traffic. The outermost loop was just prose, with corrections saved as rules in memory that could be read by every agent later in the process. Together, these loops allowed us to migrate the Messages API to Rust, which uses about 70% less CPU per request and reduces median time to first token by about 20% (Figure 15).

Keep the loops simple, so they scale with Claude’s capability. We tried to put human judgment only into what counted as correct; otherwise we left it up to Claude how to get there. Agents chose which hypotheses to test, how to reproduce each bug, and how to fix it. The verifiers judged the result. Simple loops around strong verifiers allowed us to move productively over time (Figure 16).

Move toward outer loops. At first, we had our engineers working inside the inner loop, running Claude and chasing differences themselves. Later, they moved to the seam between loops, helping to steer agents and reviewing fixes in Slack. But as the system matured, they increasingly moved to the edge, where they could provide the highest leverage, writing the rules and checks that agents worked within. As Claude grew more intelligent (and as we grew more intelligent at working with it), we evolved from directing Claude to Claude directing itself, relying on humans mainly for important judgment calls.

contentHtml:
财农〔2026〕84号

各省、自治区、直辖市财政厅（局）、农业农村（农牧）厅（局、委）、农垦管理部门、发展改革委、民（宗）委（厅、局）、林业和草原主管部门，新疆生产建设兵团财政局、农业农村局、发展和改革委员会、民族宗教事务局： 

　　按照党中央、国务院决策部署，2026年起，原衔接推进乡村振兴补助资金调整为常态化帮扶资金。在总结过渡期资金绩效评价工作经验做法的基础上，根据新要求新情况，我们制定了《常态化帮扶资金绩效评价办法》。现印发给你们，请遵照执行。

财政部 农业农村部 国家发展改革委

国家民委 国家林草局

2026年11月16日

常态化帮扶资金绩效评价办法 

　　第一条 为规范和加强常态化帮扶资金（以下简称帮扶资金）管理，根据预算绩效管理有关要求，制定本办法。 

　　第二条 本办法所称的帮扶资金是指中央、省、市、县各级财政预算安排的帮扶资金（除具体条款和指标中有特别说明外）。 

　　第三条 本办法所称帮扶资金绩效评价是对各级财政和农业农村、发展改革、民族工作、林业和草原、农垦等部门（以下统称相关部门）使用管理帮扶资金进行综合性评价。 

　　第四条 绩效评价的目标是提高资金使用效益，保障资金使用管理的安全性、规范性和有效性。 

　　第五条 绩效评价遵循以下原则： 

　　（一）聚焦任务、突出成效； 

　　（二）科学规范、公正公开； 

　　（三）分类分级、权责统一； 

　　（四）强化管理、激励约束。 

　　第六条 绩效评价的依据： 

　　（一）党中央、国务院关于常态化帮扶的方针政策； 

　　（二）预算绩效管理相关规定； 

　　（三）帮扶资金管理办法和资金项目管理有关制度； 

　　（四）常态化帮扶考核评估结果，统计部门公布的有关统计数据，以及全国常态化防止返贫致贫促乡村振兴信息系统（以下简称防止返贫致贫信息系统）、预算管理一体化系统等数据； 

　　（五）评价年度地方常态化帮扶工作情况总结； 

　　（六）资金分配下达文件及相关资料； 

　　（七）巡视巡察、监督检查、审计报告及处理决定； 

　　（八）其他相关资料。 

　　第七条 绩效评价的主要内容包括目标管理、任务管理、资金项目管理、使用效益和激励约束（加减分项）5方面。 

　　（一）目标管理。包括防止返贫致贫情况、收入增长情况等。 

　　（二）任务管理。包括资金保障、支持产业帮扶、支持就业帮扶、支持欠发达地区帮扶等。 

　　（三）资金项目管理。包括资金使用管理、项目库建设管理、项目绩效目标管理、项目质量管理、信息公开和公告公示制度落实等。 

　　（四）使用效益。包括项目推进进度、预算执行进度、项目实施成效等。 

　　（五）激励约束（加减分项）。加分项包括机制创新激励、预算执行激励、投入情况激励等；减分项包括执行中调减预算、数据质量和负面问题等。 

　　绩效评价指标体系根据评价内容设置。绩效评价的具体指标、评价内容和赋分规则，可根据常态化帮扶年度工作重点和实际情况适当调整。对各省、自治区、直辖市和新疆生产建设兵团（以下统称省）绩效评价指标体系由财政部会同其他资金管理部门设置（详见附件）。 

　　第八条 绩效评价分级实施。中央相关部门负责对各省开展帮扶资金绩效评价；省级相关部门负责组织本省帮扶资金绩效评价工作；市级相关部门负责指导县级做好帮扶资金绩效管理工作，具备条件的可按省级要求组织本市帮扶资金绩效评价工作；县级资金使用管理部门和财政部门要合理确定资金项目绩效目标并按程序报省级相关部门，作为绩效过程监控和具体项目绩效评价的依据。 

　　各级相关部门可根据工作需要，邀请或委托有关机构、专家通过调查研究、资料分析、实地评价、专家评议等方式参与帮扶资金绩效评价。 

　　第九条 对各省开展的绩效评价，由农业农村部、财政部联合其他资金管理部门明确当年绩效评价工作方案。省级相关部门联合将评价年度帮扶资金绩效自评报告等相关材料按要求报送至中央相关部门，并抄送财政部当地监管局。中央相关部门根据每年工作安排适时组织开展实地评价、专家评议和部门会审等。各省对上报材料的真实性、准确性、及时性和完整性负责。 

　　第十条 绩效评价依据所设定的指标逐项计分后确定总得分。分任务评价的指标按照各项任务的帮扶资金占比加权平均计算。根据得分将评价结果（包括整体结果和分任务结果）划分为四个等次，分别为：A（≥90分）、B（≥80分，＜90分）、C（≥60分，＜80分）、D（＜60分）。 

　　第十一条 考虑不同区域、不同部门评价指标的差异性，因少数指标不适用而满分不足百分的，按照得分折算成百分制。绩效评价结果按照东、中、西部地区分别排序。 

　　第十二条 对各省的绩效评价结果，纳入下一年度帮扶资金因素法分配，给予相应激励，由财政部、农业农村部会同其他资金管理部门联合向省级相关部门通报，并抄送省级人民政府。对绩效评价发现的问题，由农业农村部会同其他资金管理部门联合向省级相关部门反馈，并抄送财政部当地监管局。省级相关部门按照任务方向分别推动问题整改，并将整改情况按照要求由农业农村部门汇总后按程序联合报中央相关部门。 

　　地方应参照中央相关部门做法，采取适当方式反馈结果，并通过纳入帮扶资金测算因素等方式加强绩效评价结果应用。 

　　第十三条 省级财政部门会同其他资金管理部门根据绩效管理有关要求、本办法规定，结合实际情况，制定本省帮扶资金绩效评价细则，并抄送中央相关部门和财政部当地监管局。 

　　第十四条 各级相关部门及涉及工作人员在绩效评价过程中，存在违反本办法规定的，以及滥用职权、玩忽职守、徇私舞弊等违规违纪违法行为的，按照有关规定追究相应责任；涉嫌犯罪的，依法移送有关机关处理。 

　　第十五条 本办法自印发之日起施行，由财政部会同其他资金管理部门负责解释。《财政部 国家乡村振兴局 国家发展改革委 国家民委 农业农村部 国家林草局关于印发<衔接推进乡村振兴补助资金绩效评价及考核办法>的通知》（财农〔2021〕122号）、《财政部 农业农村部 国家发展改革委 国家民委 国家林草局关于修订调整衔接推进乡村振兴补助资金绩效评价相关指标的通知》（财农〔2024〕50号）同时废止。

　　附件：常态化帮扶资金绩效评价指标评分表

title: Simon Willison：过去十二个月 LLM 能力的三个转折点
originalTitle: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
summary: Simon Willison 发布其在 AI Engineer Code Summit 的主题演讲视频，提出过去十二个月 LLM 与编程智能体能力经历了三个重要转折点，并展开深入分析。文章重点回顾 Claude Opus 4.5：2026年11月24日恰为其发布一周年，Anthropic 曾称其无需手把手即可处理模糊问题、修复复杂多系统 bug，Willison 认为这些表现经受住了检验。
context: 作者 Simon Willison 是业界知名 AI 评论者，对模型能力拐点的复盘有助于判断编程智能体的演进节奏。
contentHtml:
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.

Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.

Coding agents in November 2025

Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.

In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:

Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.

This held up.

Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.

Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.

The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.

Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.

The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.

Fable class models in June/July

We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.

In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.

After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.

For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:

In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.

A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.

Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.

I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.

These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.

3D modeling and game development in September/October

Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.

I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.

3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.

Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.

I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!

Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.

Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.

Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.

The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.

It feels like another inflection point to me.

Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?

I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.

I'm getting so much done with that model right now!

It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.

Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.
